questions.hint: It is the largest solid organ, a homogeneous density filling the right upper abdomen under the diaphragm.
questions.explain: The liver fills the right upper quadrant and extends across the midline under the left hemidiaphragm. On a radiograph it is a uniform soft-tissue density whose lower edge is outlined by surrounding fat.

questions.hint: Look for a gas bubble in the left upper abdomen, under the left hemidiaphragm.
questions.explain: The stomach is a J-shaped organ in the left upper quadrant, below the left hemidiaphragm. On an erect radiograph it is seen as a gastric gas bubble, with a fluid level where the food and fluid settle.

questions.hint: The kidneys are faint bean-shaped soft-tissue shadows either side of the lumbar spine.
questions.explain: The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left because of the liver, at about T12 to L3. On a radiograph the renal outline is only visible because of the fat that surrounds it, and it is much fainter than bone.

questions.hint: It is the faint bean-shaped shadow beside the upper lumbar spine, a little higher than its partner.
questions.explain: The left kidney lies a little higher than the right, with its upper pole at about the level of T11 to T12. On a radiograph it shows as a faint oval outlined by perirenal fat, and its long axis runs parallel to the psoas muscle.

questions.hint: It is a curved soft-tissue shadow tucked under the left hemidiaphragm, beside the ribs.
questions.explain: The spleen lies under the left ninth to eleventh ribs, behind the stomach, and is protected by the ribcage. On a radiograph it is a faint smooth soft-tissue shadow at the left upper abdomen, and an enlarged spleen displaces gas in the stomach and the colon.

questions.prompt: A man with a sudden severe abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen has a thin crescent of gas under the right hemidiaphragm on an erect film. Click the organ that lies directly below the free gas.
questions.hint: Free gas collects at the highest point; the right dome of the diaphragm sits on this large solid organ.
questions.explain: Free intraperitoneal gas rises to lie between the liver and the diaphragm after a perforated peptic ulcer or viscus. On an erect radiograph a crescent of black gas lies under the hemidiaphragm, which makes the dome of the liver clearly outlined.

questions.prompt: A man has severe colicky left loin pain that spreads to the groin, and a small dense opacity is seen near the left renal outline on a plain film. Click the organ in which the stone formed.
questions.hint: Kidney stones form in the collecting system, the faint bean-shaped shadow beside the spine.
questions.explain: Most renal stones are calcium oxalate and form in the calyces and renal pelvis before passing down the ureter. On a radiograph about 90 percent are radio-opaque, a small white spot near the renal outline or along the line of the ureter.

questions.prompt: An older man develops sudden low back pain after a minor fall. A lateral film shows the front of one vertebra at the thoracolumbar junction is squashed. Click the first lumbar vertebra.
questions.hint: It is the first vertebra below the last rib-bearing thoracic vertebra.
questions.explain: L1 is the first lumbar vertebra and the usual site of the thoracolumbar junction injuries, where the conus medullaris ends at about this level. On a lateral radiograph the vertebral body is wedge-shaped when compressed and the endplate looks dense.

questions.hint: It is the last and biggest of the lumbar vertebrae, sitting on top of the sacrum.
questions.explain: The fifth lumbar vertebra has the largest body, and its wedge shape creates the lumbosacral angle where it joins the sacrum. On a lateral radiograph it is the bottom vertebra of the lumbar column, resting on the first sacral segment.

questions.hint: It is the large flared bone of the pelvis, made of the ilium, ischium and pubis.
questions.explain: The hip bone is formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis, and the three meet at the acetabulum. On a radiograph the pelvic brim, ilium and acetabulum form a dense continuous white ring on each side.

questions.hint: It is the triangular bone at the bottom of the spine, between the two hip bones.
questions.explain: The sacrum is five fused vertebrae that wedge between the iliac bones to form the sacroiliac joints. On a frontal radiograph it is a triangle whose centre is crossed by the sacral foramina, which show as paired round lucencies.

questions.prompt: An older woman falls at home and cannot weight-bear; the left leg is shortened and externally rotated. A pelvic film shows a break through the neck of one bone. Click the bone that is fractured.
questions.hint: It is the long bone of the thigh, whose head fits into the acetabulum.
questions.explain: Fractures of the femoral neck threaten the blood supply from the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery. On a radiograph look for a break in the cortex, a break in Shenton's line and a shortened leg.

questions.prompt: On a plain abdominal film, a patient with a suspected retroperitoneal abscess loses the normal sharp edge of the psoas shadow on the right. Click the muscle whose outline is lost.
questions.hint: The shadow runs obliquely beside the lumbar spine from the upper lumbar region to the groin.
questions.explain: The psoas major arises from the lumbar vertebrae and joins iliacus to cross the pelvic brim, and it is outlined by retroperitoneal fat. On a radiograph the psoas margin is a thin straight line on either side of the spine, and fluid or a mass blurs it.

questions.hint: It frames the abdomen, and its gas and faecal mottling mark it from the smaller central bowel.
questions.explain: The large bowel frames the abdomen with its caecum on the right, its transverse colon in the middle and the descending colon on the left, and has haustra. On a radiograph it is recognised by its peripheral position and gas, with a mottled pattern of faeces.

questions.hint: It is a rounded soft-tissue shadow in the midline just above the pubic bones.
questions.explain: The bladder is a muscular reservoir in the pelvis, behind the pubic symphysis and in front of the rectum. On a radiograph a full bladder is a smooth, faint, rounded soft-tissue density in the midline of the pelvis, between the hip bones.
